Building a Versioned In Memory Store

A versioned store connects ownership, errors, shared data, and concurrency. Readers need stable views; writers must avoid publishing half a transaction. The design must define stale snapshots, conflicts, and safe retries. Rust can enforce exclusive access to commit, but it cannot choose the consistency model.
We will build a process-local key-value store with immutable snapshots and optimistic transactions. The implementation is intentionally

conservative. Every committed write advances one global version. A transaction can commit only when that version still matches the version from which it began. This rejects some nonconflicting writes, but makes the validation rule easy to state and inspect. It is a useful first design because its correctness argument fits in a few explicit steps.

This store is not durable: it has no write-ahead log, crash recovery, replication, or remote transaction protocol. Commit means only that this in-memory object accepted a state. Valid Rust references cannot turn that result into durable acceptance.

A snapshot contains an immutable map and the version associated with that map. The store owns one Arc to the current map. Readers clone that Arc, so an old map remains available while readers use it. Writers create a replacement map and publish it only after validation. Existing snapshots continue to observe the old map.

The map stores owned keys and values. This avoids borrowing from request buffers or temporary transactions. Values could instead be Arc<[u8]> to make map copies cheaper for large payloads. That change would alter copying cost, but it would not alter the conflict rule. Separating these questions is valuable: consistency concerns which versions may commit; representation concerns how much work those versions require.

A transaction owns its staged changes and a snapshot of its starting state. Reads first consult staged changes and then the snapshot. A staged deletion must be distinguishable from no staged change, so the staging map stores Option<String> values. Some(value) means replacement and None means deletion. The outer map lookup tells us whether the transaction has an entry at all.

The following program has no external dependencies. commit requires &mut self, so safe callers cannot publish two commits through the same store simultaneously. Wrapping the store in a mutex would extend that serialization to multiple threads. The global version check remains necessary because transactions can be created, held independently, and submitted later.

Validation checks both the global version and the identity of the snapshot's map. The pointer-identity check matters because two different stores can have the same numeric version. Without it, a transaction could read one store and commit to another. A durable or distributed implementation would normally use an explicit store identity and a version protocol appropriate to its storage model.

There are four important transitions. Before validation, the transaction is only a proposal. After validation, the new map is prepared privately. Publishing replaces the store's map pointer. Updating the version completes the new state before the mutable borrow is released. No user callback executes between pointer replacement and version update, and those assignments themselves do not allocate. A reader cannot interleave through a safe shared reference while this mutable borrow is active.

Building a replacement first gives a strong structural benefit: ordinary panics during preparation do not partially update the currently published map. The example uses strings and their ordinary ordering. A more generic key type can execute user-defined comparison code; that is another reason to keep preparation separate from publication. Allocation failure may abort the process under the allocator's policy, so an argument about unwind safety does not establish recovery from every failure mode.
Understand What the Global Version Proves

If a transaction commits, no earlier writer has changed the store since the transaction's snapshot was taken. Therefore all of its snapshot reads correspond to the state immediately preceding its commit. Its staged changes can be applied as one serialized operation in commit order. This is a conservative serializable execution model for these transactions, provided all relevant reads and writes occur through the store.

The final condition is easy to overlook. Suppose the transaction reads a balance from this store but obtains an exchange rate from a mutable external cache. The store's version says nothing about the exchange rate. A proof is only as broad as the state it actually validates. Application invariants that depend on time, files, remote services, or another database require an additional protocol.

The conservative model also rejects harmless overlaps. Two transactions that write different keys still conflict when the first commits. This can be acceptable for a small configuration service with infrequent writes. It can be expensive for a high-volume independent-counter workload. Correctness comes before granularity: establish a model whose invariants are clear, then measure whether its conflicts justify a more complicated validator.

Read-only transactions currently validate their version too. A read-only transaction submitted after a writer receives a conflict even though it has no effects. One alternative is to return its snapshot version without validation. That is appropriate when a historical consistent read is sufficient. It is inappropriate if the caller interprets a successful validation as evidence that a decision still reflects the current state. Method names should make that distinction visible.

Per-key versions can reduce conflicts, but tracking only written keys is insufficient when decisions depend on reads. Imagine two operators who may be on call, with an invariant that at least one remains. Two transactions each observe both operators, then each removes a different operator. Their write sets are disjoint. Validating only write-write conflicts allows both to commit and breaks the invariant.

A finer optimistic design records the versions of all keys read and validates them at commit. Missing keys need a representation too. If a transaction reads that a key is absent, another transaction inserts it, and the first relies on the absence, the validator must detect that change. Deletion and reinsertion can create another trap when a generation number is reused. Use monotonically advancing versions or another identity mechanism that does not silently equate different histories.

Range queries are harder still. Recording the versions of returned keys does not detect a new matching key that was absent during the original query. That is a phantom. A range-level generation, predicate lock, index validation, or another explicitly designed mechanism is needed if range-dependent decisions require serializable behavior. A BTreeMap gives ordered traversal; it does not automatically give a database isolation level.

These issues illustrate the boundary between Rust correctness and algorithm correctness. The compiler can establish that a map reference is not used after invalidation. It cannot infer that a transaction forgot to validate the absence of an operator. Tests should describe the application invariant directly and arrange schedules that attempt to violate it.

An Arc snapshot is cheap to create but can be expensive to retain. The current map may be replaced many times while an old snapshot keeps one historical map alive. The example clones all key and value strings for every write transaction, so peak memory includes every still-retained version plus the replacement under construction. This is predictable but can be substantial.

Structural sharing can reduce copying. A persistent tree copies only changed paths while sharing unchanged nodes. Its ownership graph is more complex, but Arc can represent shared immutable nodes. Another design stores large values behind Arc while cloning the top-level map. That preserves a simple validator and reduces payload copying without implementing an entirely new collection.

Reference counting itself is not free. Cloning Arc updates a shared count, and dropping the final reference runs destruction. If the last reader releases a huge historical map on a latency-sensitive thread, that thread

may pay the destruction cost. Some systems deliberately defer reclamation to another thread. Such a change needs a bounded retirement policy; otherwise delayed reclamation merely becomes another unbounded queue.
The complete example below shows the essential snapshot behavior with copy-on-write. It is a separate experiment, not an optimization already present in the store implementation.

When another strong owner exists, copy-on-write must preserve that owner's view. Do not assume Arc::make_mut avoids cloning under a snapshot-heavy workload. Measure the actual number of live readers at write time. A representation optimization can be ineffective precisely when the versioning feature is most heavily used.

After a conflict, a caller may begin another transaction and repeat its computation. Repeating pure calculations is usually straightforward. Repeating external effects is not. If the transaction sent an email before commit, retrying can send it twice even though only one state change is accepted. If it charged a payment before commit, the consequences are larger.

One useful pattern computes a proposal and an effect description without executing the effect. Commit both the state change and a durable or otherwise appropriate outbox record in the same consistency domain, then process the outbox with deduplication. Our in-memory store cannot make

that outbox survive process failure, so it is only an illustration of where the protocol belongs. Another approach uses an external service's idempotency key and records its result under a carefully specified recovery protocol.

A retry policy also needs a limit. Immediate retries under contention can create repeated work and poor tail latency. Backoff, admission control, or a serialized command processor may be more effective than increasingly fine validation. Optimistic concurrency is attractive when conflicts are rare and transactions are cheap. It becomes less attractive when every failed transaction performs expensive work that must be discarded.

Returning the consumed transaction inside CommitError can help callers inspect or reuse a proposal. It should not imply that the old reads are still valid. A safer retry API accepts a closure that reruns the whole read-compute-write step against a fresh snapshot, while clearly restricting external side effects. Even that closure-based API cannot prove semantic idempotence through an ordinary trait bound.

Name every queue and owner before designing a worker pipeline. Who owns queued work? What happens when a worker fails? Who drains results while the producer is blocked? Does shutdown discard work or finish it? Is the bound in messages or bytes? These are independent contracts hidden by the pipeline's simple shape.

We will build a finite pipeline using standard-library scoped threads and bounded channels. A coordinator distributes numeric jobs among workers. Each worker computes one result and sends it to a collector. The collector reduces results into a summary instead of retaining every result. This makes the buffering behavior visible and avoids requiring a runtime or an external channel implementation.

The pipeline's domain is intentionally pure arithmetic. That lets us reason about ownership transfer and lifecycle without confusing successful computation with durable side effects. Later sections explain what changes when a job sends a network request or modifies storage.

The pipeline has one bounded input channel per worker and one shared bounded output channel. Each worker owns its receiver. The coordinator owns the input senders. The collector owns the output receiver. Workers own clones of the output sender. The coordinator drops the original output sender once worker creation is complete.

The extra collector thread is essential. If the coordinator filled every input queue before starting to drain a bounded output queue, workers could block while sending results, stop receiving jobs, and leave the coordinator blocked while sending jobs. Every component would be waiting for another component to free capacity. Bounded queues expose this wait cycle; they do not solve it by themselves.

coordinator -> worker input queues -> workers -> result queue -> collector
      |                                                    |
      +---------------- final joins -----------------------+

In this design the collector runs while dispatch is active, so output pressure can be relieved independently. Worker input queues eventually have space if each computation finishes and the collector continues consuming. That is a progress argument under stated assumptions. It is not a claim that the operating system guarantees fair scheduling or that an arbitrary user callback cannot block forever.

This example returns a summary or an error for invalid worker counts, dispatch failure, or a joined thread panic. If the OS cannot create a thread, Scope::spawn panics. Use Builder::spawn_scoped for a returned startup error and close the channels for any workers already started. The summary counts failed squares separately from overflow in the aggregate sum.
The example is finite and assumes the counts fit in usize, which is practical for the demonstration but still a representation assumption. A production
long-running collector should use checked or saturating counters according to its metric policy. The numeric range of a job is independent of the numeric range of a metric counting jobs.

Round-robin routing is simple and deterministic, but it can leave the coordinator waiting on a slow worker while another worker is idle. That is head-of-line blocking in the dispatcher. A shared work queue or work-stealing scheduler can improve utilization for uneven jobs. Changing the scheduling policy should preserve the ownership and shutdown contracts established here.

Normal shutdown begins when dispatch finishes and the coordinator drops all job senders. A worker continues receiving buffered jobs, then sees the channel disconnected once its queue is empty. It exits and drops its result sender. After every worker has exited, no result sender remains, so the collector drains the last buffered results and ends its loop. The coordinator joins workers and then the collector.

The order in which values disappear is the shutdown protocol. There is no special stop message in this version. That is appropriate because the desired policy is to finish all work already accepted by the input channels. A stop message could accidentally sit behind ordinary work, and multiple worker queues would require separate stop messages. Channel closure already expresses that no additional work will arrive.

Dropping the original result sender is easy to miss. If the coordinator retained that sender while joining the collector, the collector could wait forever for another result even after every worker finished. The channel remains connected because an unused sender is still an owner. This is a lifecycle bug that the type system permits: the ownership is valid, but the program's waiting policy is wrong.

The join pass retains worker panic payloads until the collector has joined. This arithmetic example can then drop ordinary panic payloads. If you adapt the pipeline to run arbitrary callbacks, choose a disposal policy as in Level 28. Implicit scope joins enforce lifetimes and can panic when a child has failed.

If a worker panics, its receiver is dropped. Sending to that worker then fails and returns ownership of the undelivered job inside the send error. This example discards that error payload and returns an infrastructure failure after cleanup. A more capable implementation could recover that specific job and route it elsewhere: the failed send did not deliver it to the worker. Previously accepted or active jobs are different. A worker may have performed an external effect for one of those before panicking, so recovering the undelivered message does not establish the retry status of earlier work.

Each input channel stores at most two queued u64 jobs. Each worker may hold one active job and one pending result. The result queue stores at most eight results. The coordinator may hold one job while waiting to send. The collector holds a small summary. Thread stacks and channel implementation overhead also consume memory, and creating an arbitrary number of workers would make that overhead unbounded with respect to the job count.

This is a bound on live queue entries, not a universal bound on bytes for arbitrary message types. Replacing u64 with String permits one message to own a large allocation. Replacing it with Arc<Vec<u8>> can keep a shared large allocation alive even when only one small handle is queued. A byte budget may need a semaphore or explicit accounting carried by each message.

There is another subtle source of unboundedness: the producer. If the caller constructs a vector containing all jobs before calling the pipeline, bounded internal channels do not bound that vector. This implementation generates values incrementally from a range. Real systems should inspect the entire path from input acquisition through result retention, not only the most visible queue.

The collector's reduction is also deliberate. If it instead stored every output in a vector, output memory would grow with the workload even though every channel stayed bounded. That can be correct for a finite batch with an explicit output budget. It should not be described as a constant-memory streaming pipeline.
Ordering and Throughput Pull in Different Directions

Results arrive in channel delivery order. A worker can finish first and pause before sending. When sum_overflowed is set, the partial sum is incomplete, and skipping overflowing additions can make it depend on delivery order. To restore input order, give each job a sequence number and let the collector buffer out-of-order results. A slow early job can force the collector to retain many later results.

Bounded reorder storage creates an additional progress question. If the collector stops draining the shared output queue because its reorder buffer is full, the slow job may eventually try to send into that same full queue. A naive policy can deadlock even though all computations finish. Possible repairs include a bounded window of dispatched sequence numbers, separate control paths, or a scheduling rule that ensures the missing earliest result can always be delivered.

Do not add sequence numbers and assume ordering is solved. Decide the maximum distance between the oldest incomplete job and the newest admitted job. That distance controls both reorder memory and the amount of speculative work. Some applications can process results in delivery order and avoid reorder storage. When input order is part of the user-visible contract, give it an explicit budget.

Throughput measurements should separate computation from coordination. Tiny jobs can spend most of their time transferring through channels. Batching several items per message may help, but increases the work retained by one blocked sender and the delay before a partially filled batch is processed. Batch size is another latency-memory-throughput tradeoff, not an unconditional optimization.

A graceful drain means finish accepted work. Immediate cancellation means stop as soon as possible and account for abandoned work. These are different protocols. An atomic cancellation flag can tell a worker to stop before the next job, but it does not wake a worker blocked indefinitely in recv, and it does not interrupt arbitrary blocking I/O already in progress.

Closing the input channels wakes receivers when their queues are drained or disconnected, but it does not necessarily discard queued jobs. A worker can check a cancellation flag after receiving and choose to abandon the job. The component holding that job must then record whether it was cancelled, retried, or intentionally lost. Merely returning from the thread hides that distinction.

Timeouts create uncertainty around external effects. A worker may time out while a remote server continues processing a request. Retrying that job may duplicate the effect. Useful job envelopes often contain a stable operation identifier, an attempt number, and a domain-specific idempotency key. The pipeline can transport those values, but the remote protocol must actually honor them.

For a service, acceptance should have a precise point. Is a job accepted when received from the socket, when inserted into an internal queue, or when durably recorded? A bounded channel can acknowledge only process-local transfer. If the process crashes afterward, the message may be lost. Rust's ownership transfer is exact about memory responsibility and silent about durable delivery unless the application adds that mechanism.
Test the Lifecycle Rather Than the Scheduler

Tests should assert observable contracts under deliberately constrained conditions. Use one worker and capacity zero to expose rendezvous behavior. Pause one worker after computing to control delivery order. Inject a job error without panicking and verify later work completes. Inject a panic in a controlled test and verify the coordinator returns. Use test timeouts to catch lifecycle regressions that could otherwise wait indefinitely.

Avoid tests that require a particular interleaving merely because it happened once. A sleep can encourage an interleaving but is a weak synchronization primitive. Barriers, additional test channels, or instrumented hooks can establish the exact state before triggering a failure. For example, wait until a worker has received a job, then close the result receiver and verify the worker handles a failed send.

Here, accepted equals completed plus failed plus abandoned. External effects need an uncertain category until reconciled. Lab D carries that accounting through one request's full path.

A protocol can begin with an enum named State and grow into repeated checks across many methods. One checks negotiation, another checks shutdown, and a third assumes an assigned identifier. As the protocol grows, those checks can drift apart. The representation should make their relationship visible.

Rust offers several ways to represent these conditions. An enum can represent a runtime state and force exhaustive handling of its variants. A generic state parameter can make different operations available on

different types. Ownership can make a transition consume the previous state, preventing later use of the old capability. These techniques are most useful when they expose the actual protocol, including failure and retry behavior.

This level develops a local model of a framed connection. It is not a networking implementation. Its transport records frames in memory so that the ownership and state transitions are visible without an I/O runtime. We will then examine what changes when a transition sends bytes to another process, where local type changes alone cannot establish remote agreement.

A connection is initially negotiating. Successful negotiation permits data frames. Closing consumes that permission. The important question is what evidence justifies each transition. A local caller passing a supported version is evidence only in this model. A real connection would need to validate a received peer message, perhaps after several reads and writes.

The state type should therefore describe a fact the implementation has established, rather than a fact the caller merely wishes were true. If a public constructor can create Connection<Established> without negotiation, the type no longer proves negotiation happened. Private fields and controlled constructors are part of the design.

State also includes runtime data. An established connection needs a next sequence number. Using a marker type alone would hide that relationship in an unrelated optional field. Instead, the established state owns the counter it needs. The negotiating state owns its offer count. The closed state owns neither because no further protocol operation is permitted.

The model below keeps unsupported negotiation recoverable by returning the original connection. Data send validates its arguments before changing the sequence number. Closing consumes the established connection and returns a closed value whose transcript can be inspected.

The method sets differ between states. There is no send method on a negotiating or closed connection. There is no successful way to keep using the original established connection after close, because closing takes
ownership. An alias to the same resource would undermine that exclusivity, so the connection itself is not cloneable.

The error returns the unsent payload. This is often preferable to discarding a caller-owned buffer on a validation failure. It also makes a useful distinction: the error means the local model did not enqueue a data frame. A real transport error might occur after some bytes were written and could not make the same promise without tracking write progress.

The model rejects a send when incrementing the sequence would overflow. Consequently the maximum integer value is never used as a frame sequence. That is an explicit exhaustion policy. An alternative could use the maximum once and transition to an exhausted state. Wrapping silently would reuse identifiers and could confuse duplicate detection, so it should not be introduced casually as an arithmetic convenience.

An established connection is a capability to emit data under the modeled protocol. Consuming it during close revokes that capability locally. This is more precise than a Boolean checked on every send, but it also changes ergonomics. Callers must handle a different return type, and a container cannot store all states under one concrete generic instantiation.

That is a useful trade when application control flow already has clear phases. A setup function can return an established resource. A worker can own it for the duration of a session. Shutdown can consume it and return a report. The compiler then helps prevent phase confusion across those boundaries.

Typestate becomes less convenient when many independently scheduled events can change the state at runtime. A connection manager may store thousands of connections in different phases. Representing the manager as a generic type for every possible combination would be impractical. An enum containing state-specific structures is usually a better representation at that boundary.

The two approaches can cooperate. A dynamic manager matches on a runtime enum and invokes phase-specific methods on the contained typed resource. That preserves a finite runtime representation while keeping
each state's operations locally precise. The objective is to make illegal transitions hard to express in the part of the program that performs them, not to maximize the number of generic parameters.

The next complete example uses an owned enum to represent a request that can be started or completed. Failed transitions return the original request unchanged. This makes the rejected event recoverable and keeps ownership explicit.

Taking ownership lets a transition move payloads between variants without cloning. A transition taking &mut self needs a replacement, an Option, or another representation to move the payload out. Its temporary state must remain safe if execution panics. Taking self is often simpler when the caller can handle the returned state.

Returning Err(original) is not always the right policy. A malformed network event may require closing the connection rather than preserving the old state. A timeout may move a request into an indeterminate state because the peer could have accepted it. The return type should express those possibilities directly. Using the same generic error for every failed transition can erase the most important information.
Local State and Remote State Can Diverge

Consider sending a close frame over a socket. The local method may serialize the frame, write some bytes, and then encounter an error. Did the peer receive the close? It may have received all of it even if the local operation failed to observe completion. Dropping the local connection cannot answer that question. A Closed marker proves only the condition that the implementation actually establishes.

Useful protocols often distinguish closing, locally closed, peer acknowledged, and fully finished. Whether all these states need separate Rust types depends on which distinctions affect allowed operations. If application code may retry a close but may not send more data, a closing state with a retry method can be appropriate. If the resource will simply be discarded, a detailed public state machine may add complexity without changing useful behavior.

The same issue appears with requests. A cancelled future may have written a request completely before being dropped. Retrying with a new identifier can execute the request twice. Retrying with the same identifier only helps if the peer stores and recognizes that identifier under the required failure conditions. Types can carry the identifier through transitions, but they cannot create a deduplication guarantee on the remote side.

This is why protocol review should include a table of observable events and uncertain outcomes. For each write, timeout, disconnect, and cancellation, ask what the local endpoint knows and what the peer may have done. An
unknown outcome is a legitimate state. Pretending it is a simple failure often causes incorrect automatic retries.
Cancellation Must Leave a Representable State

An async transition may suspend after modifying local state or after sending part of a frame. If the future owns the connection and is dropped, dropping the connection may be an acceptable cancellation policy. If the future merely borrows the connection, cancellation must leave the borrowed object in a state that later methods understand.

One robust approach stores write progress in the connection itself. The future advances an offset into an owned frame buffer. If cancelled, the offset and buffer remain, and a later operation can resume or explicitly abort the connection. Another approach makes the resource unusable for further protocol traffic after any interrupted write. That is simpler but should be visible in the API's failure behavior.

Avoid placing indispensable progress only in a temporary future while leaving the connection marked established. Dropping that future could lose the information needed to continue the byte stream correctly. This is a semantic invariant, even if the underlying memory remains safe. The cancellation analysis from the async levels applies directly to state-machine representation.

Dropping a connection also cannot perform arbitrary asynchronous cleanup. A destructor can release local resources, but it cannot wait through ordinary async suspension points. If graceful protocol completion matters, provide an explicit async close operation and define what ordinary drop does when close is skipped. Blocking indefinitely inside drop would move the problem into unrelated scopes and can deadlock an executor thread.

It is tempting to encode every independent property as a generic parameter: authenticated, compressed, encrypted, writable, registered, draining. Six Boolean properties already describe sixty-four combinations before runtime counters enter the picture. Many combinations may be impossible, but the public API can still become difficult to name and understand.

Group properties that transition together into one semantic state. Keep independent runtime policy in ordinary fields when it does not affect method availability. Use newtypes for important validated values such as a nonempty stream identifier or checked frame length. A small number of meaningful capabilities usually communicates more than a large product of marker parameters.

Error design can simplify the state space as well. If any transport failure permanently invalidates a session, consuming the session and returning an error is honest and easy to reason about. If recovery is required, return the exact recoverable resource. Do not force a complex recovery type into an API whose callers always discard it, and do not hide a recoverable buffer when callers genuinely need to retry.

Testing should follow transitions and invariants. Generate sequences of events and assert that accepted transitions preserve identifier uniqueness, frame ordering, and resource accounting. Compile-fail tests can check that a closed typed connection has no send operation. Runtime tests must still examine malformed peer messages and interrupted I/O because those enter through values rather than through the method set.
1. Modify the local connection model so the maximum u32 sequence number may be used exactly once. Decide whether exhaustion is a field inside the established state or a separate state type.
2. Design an async write operation that may be cancelled after a partial write. Specify which object owns the frame and offset, and which subsequent operations remain legal.

3. A manager must store both negotiating and established connections. Design an enum boundary that permits polling either state while exposing data send only after the established variant has been matched.

1. Store Option<u32> as the next sequence, taking Some(max) for the last send and replacing it with None. Future sends return exhaustion without emitting a frame. A separate exhausted type gives a stronger method distinction but complicates a method that normally borrows &mut self; it is most useful if callers benefit from owning the exhausted resource explicitly.

2. Put the frame buffer and current offset in the connection's pending-write state. A future borrows and advances that state. After cancellation, allow only resuming the pending write or aborting the connection until framing is restored. Do not allow a new data frame to interleave with the unfinished bytes.

3. Use an enum with variants containing Connection<Negotiating> and Connection<Established>, plus any closing states required by the protocol. A match gives access to the state-specific value. Transition code consumes one variant and returns another; rejected negotiation either restores the negotiating resource or produces a terminal error according to policy.

• Drop documents synchronous destruction and its role in resource cleanup.

Design a client-side command state machine for a fake peer. The peer may execute a command and then lose its reply. The client supports reconnect, querying status when the peer protocol permits it, and an explicit retry policy. Choose which transitions should consume typed capabilities and which belong in a runtime enum. A disconnect after sending must not automatically become a confirmed failure. Define the stable operation ID, the peer's deduplication or status-retention contract, and what happens when that retention expires. Build a deterministic simulation of lost acknowledgment, duplicate delivery, and confirmed rejection before execution. Explain what your Rust types guarantee locally and what remains dependent on the peer's behavior.

A crate makes promises beyond compiling in the author's preferred configuration. Downstream users depend on its public types, supported compilers, feature combinations, platforms, and dependency compatibility. Those promises are part of the architecture because other programs compile against them.

This level follows a fictional protocol library named framecore. Its central algorithm validates and describes frames. Some users run it in a server with the standard library. Others want the same frame logic in a constrained environment without operating-system services. The goal is to share a coherent semantic core while keeping transport integration and deployment policy outside that core.

The design questions begin after cargo new: where should a boundary sit, which obligations does a feature change, and what evidence supports compatibility? Build configuration is executable architecture. One manifest field can enable paths the usual development build never checks.

The frame model should own validation rules, lengths, identifiers, and structured protocol errors. A socket adapter should own reads, writes, buffering, and cancellation behavior. A service should own admission control, retries, logging policy, and shutdown. These layers may live in separate crates when independent dependency or platform requirements justify it. They need not become separate crates merely to imitate a diagram.

One advantage of a small protocol core is that it can be tested without a runtime or network. Another is that its public API need not expose runtime-specific error types or buffer implementations. If an adapter returns a framework's concrete buffer in every public method, that framework becomes part of the library's compatibility surface. Replacing it later can affect downstream code even when the protocol semantics stay identical.

Avoid making the lowest layer artificially generic over every imaginable transport. A byte-slice decoder and an owned frame encoder may be sufficient. Adapters can combine them with their own I/O abstractions. A generic transport trait belongs in the core only when the core genuinely needs to drive transport operations and when its error, lifetime, and async contracts are clear.

There is also a cost to splitting crates. Each crate has a manifest, version, feature graph, documentation surface, and release relationship. A private module can provide encapsulation without introducing those
responsibilities. Start from dependencies and independent consumers, then decide whether separate compilation and distribution boundaries are useful.

Cargo features are combined across a dependency graph. A library should generally design them as additive capabilities so two downstream users can enable different features without making the shared dependency unusable. A feature that silently changes the meaning of an existing operation is harder to compose than one that exposes an additional adapter.

For framecore, std can enable operating-system adapters. Error types can implement core::error::Error in either configuration. The trace feature depends on std for diagnostics. Frame validation follows the same protocol in every build.
This illustrative manifest is a project configuration excerpt. Its version and compiler baseline are choices for this example, not a claim about the newest available toolchain.

[package]
name = "framecore"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"
rust-version = "1.85"

[features]
default = ["std"]
std = []
trace = ["std"]

The baseline here would need to be tested before publication. Merely writing rust-version does not prove the source and every dependency actually build on that compiler. Our book examples are checked on the locally available compiler identified in the reading guide; that is separate from the hypothetical crate's support policy.

Mutually exclusive features deserve particular caution. Suppose one feature selects backend A and another selects backend B by defining the same public implementation twice. A downstream graph can enable both

even if each direct user enables only one. Prefer exposing both adapters under distinct names or choosing a backend through an explicit type or constructor. If exclusivity is unavoidable, document the composition limit and detect it clearly, but recognize that it restricts downstream use.

Defaults are conveniences, not a reliable global off switch. One dependency can request no default features while another enables them. Review the resolved graph when behavior surprises you. The relevant unit is the dependency instance and Cargo's resolver rules, not just the line in one manifest.

The following complete library example demonstrates a core that needs neither allocation nor operating-system services. It accepts only lengths that can be represented in a four-byte length field and computes total encoded size with checked arithmetic. Optional tracing does not change the result.

The two errors are distinct because a payload length may fit the protocol field while header plus payload exceeds the platform's addressable usize range. On common wide platforms the second branch is unreachable after the first check, but the source expresses the platform-independent contract. Tests on a wide host alone do not exercise every narrow-target boundary.

no_std does not mean no heap, no runtime support of any kind, or suitability for every embedded target. It changes the automatically linked standard-library environment. A library may separately use alloc when an allocator is available. Target support also depends on atomic availability, panic strategy, linker setup, and any foreign dependencies. Document the actual requirements rather than using no_std as a broad performance or deployment claim.

The trace is best effort. A failed write leaves the length result intact. Writing to standard error can still block. A reusable library can let the application choose the diagnostic sink and timing policy. Test the relevant feature combinations when tracing affects timing or synchronization.

If a public function returns a type from another crate, downstream users may need that same crate version to name, construct, or match the result. Two incompatible versions of a dependency define distinct Rust types even when their displayed names look identical. This becomes especially visible in plugin systems, serialization adapters, and public error enums containing foreign error types.

A wrapper can reduce exposure, but it must preserve the operations callers need. Wrapping every useful type behind an opaque handle may force users into awkward conversions or eliminate zero-copy access. Review the boundary from both sides: which dependency details are incidental, and which are intentionally part of the API?

Auto traits also participate in the promise. A future returned by a function may be expected to be Send. A public type may currently be Sync because of its fields. Adding a non-thread-safe field later can break downstream uses even if no method signature changes. The API levels explain these
implications at the type level; release engineering must actually check them across intended changes.

Error evolution needs the same care. An exhaustive public enum makes adding a variant a source-compatibility concern. A non-exhaustive enum leaves room for additional variants but requires downstream wildcard handling. Hiding all structure in a string is easy to evolve but prevents reliable programmatic recovery. Choose based on expected caller decisions, not only on implementation convenience.
Build Scripts Cross Another Execution Boundary

A build script runs on the build host and may generate source, probe libraries, or invoke native compilers. The final library may target a different platform. Confusing host and target assumptions can produce generated constants or linker flags that work locally and fail in cross-compilation.

Keep generated output in the designated output directory and make input dependencies explicit. A generator that reads an undeclared schema or environment variable can leave stale output after a change. A generator that embeds the current time can make equivalent builds differ even when source inputs are identical. Reproducibility requires deciding which inputs are legitimate and how they are recorded.

Build dependencies are executable dependencies. A procedural macro and a build script can run code during compilation, before the resulting application starts. Reviewing only runtime dependencies therefore misses part of the supply chain. A smaller dependency set can reduce review and build cost, but rewriting mature functionality locally can introduce its own correctness burden. Evaluate the actual code and maintenance requirements.

Native integration adds another version axis: headers, libraries, target ABI, and compiler flags must agree. A successful Rust type check cannot establish that a linked C library uses the expected structure layout. The FFI level's ownership and ABI contracts continue to apply during packaging and deployment.
Define a Support Matrix With Evidence

A useful continuous integration matrix follows supported claims. If the crate supports the minimum compiler, test it. If it supports no default features, compile and test that configuration. If adapters are optional, exercise each supported adapter and meaningful combinations. If the crate promises multiple targets, include target-specific compilation and runtime tests where execution is available.

Testing only --all-features is insufficient. Code excluded by the maximal configuration can contain broken imports or missing bounds. Testing only the default configuration misses optional integrations. At the same time, testing every mathematical subset becomes impractical as features grow. Reduce the configuration space by designing additive features and identify representative combinations from real dependency interactions.

The following command sequence is a starting point for this fictional crate, not a universal complete matrix. A project with foreign libraries, runtime integrations, or platform-specific behavior needs additional checks tied to those promises.

cargo test --locked
cargo test --locked --no-default-features
cargo test --locked --all-features
cargo check --locked --all-targets
cargo doc --locked --no-deps
cargo package --locked

--locked asks Cargo to use the recorded dependency resolution rather than updating it as part of the command. This improves repeatability for that resolution, but it does not by itself make the entire build hermetic. Compiler versions, target toolchains, native libraries, environment inputs, and build scripts can still matter.

Package validation catches another class of problems: files present in a development checkout may be absent from the distributed package. Examples may reference a workspace-only path. Generated code may depend on an untracked file. Reviewing and building the actual packaged artifact tests the boundary that users receive.

Examples should demonstrate the intended ownership path. If every example clones a buffer before calling the API, investigate whether the API forces unnecessary ownership or whether the example hides an important borrow. If every error is unwrapped, readers cannot see which failures are expected and which are invariant violations.

Document the dimensions that types do not express: cancellation behavior, allocation behavior where promised, ordering, blocking, fairness, panic conditions, and external side effects. Avoid promising exact implementation details unless callers need them. A documented guarantee can become a compatibility obligation even when no compiler checks it.

Rustdoc examples can compile as tests, which helps prevent drift. Compile-fail examples can show forbidden usage, but a test that merely fails for any reason may pass after an unrelated syntax error. Keep rejected examples small and inspect the intended diagnostic category during maintenance. The book's example checks follow this distinction between accepted programs, rejected programs, and nonstandalone sketches.

Finally, release notes should explain behavior changes from the caller's perspective. A new internal data structure matters when it changes latency, allocation, ordering, or requirements. A compiler baseline change matters even if the runtime behavior stays identical. A clear compatibility story is a technical feature because it lets downstream developers make reliable integration decisions.

1. Your library's default feature enables a network adapter. Two downstream dependencies disagree about whether defaults should be enabled. Explain the likely composition and redesign the feature layout if the core must remain usable without networking.

2. A public future becomes non-Send after a refactor introduces Rc across an await point. Describe a regression check that captures the intended API property without depending on the future's concrete anonymous type.
3. A build script generates protocol constants from a schema file and an environment variable. Specify the declared inputs, generated output location, and cross-compilation considerations.

1. One user's request can enable the default feature for the shared dependency, so another user's disabled defaults do not necessarily remove it. Keep the core independent, make networking an explicit additive adapter feature, and avoid changing core validation semantics when networking is enabled. Inspect the resolved feature graph when diagnosing integration behavior.

2. Write a compile-time helper accepting T: Send and pass the returned future into it using representative borrowed inputs. The check tests the property callers need while leaving the concrete future opaque. Add separate checks for any intended lifetime constraints; Send alone does not imply 'static.

3. Declare schema and environment changes as rerun triggers, write generated files under OUT_DIR, and distinguish host execution from target properties. Use target configuration supplied by the build environment rather than assuming the host's sizes or ABI describe the target. Keep nondeterministic data out of generated protocol constants.

Understanding advanced Rust includes explaining a design after the compiler accepts it. Accepted programs can still deadlock, break domain rules, allocate without bound, duplicate effects, or hide an unsound abstraction. Review follows invariants across ownership boundaries and asks what evidence supports each promise.

This level reviews two small safe Rust designs: a transfer and a cache. Each connects capabilities, state changes, failures, and caller observations. Lab D then follows one request through a parser, bounded dispatch, versioned ledger, peer uncertainty, and drain report. Use that worked bridge before building the final campaign's variation.
Begin With the Claim a Caller Relies On

A function signature is a partial contract. &mut Store establishes exclusive access through that borrow. It does not establish that a transaction preserves a balance invariant. Result<T, E> exposes failure, but it does not say whether an error leaves the input unchanged. Arc<T> shares ownership, but it does not establish a bounded retention policy or make arbitrary interior state thread-safe.

Write the semantic claim in a sentence that can be contradicted by an example. For a transfer function: if it returns an error, balances are unchanged; if it succeeds, the requested amount moved between two distinct valid accounts without arithmetic overflow. For a cache: returned values remain valid independently of later map mutation, and loading does not hold the cache lock. These claims are more useful than saying the code is clean or idiomatic.

Next identify all operations that can interrupt progress: ordinary errors, panics, cancellation points, callbacks, blocking I/O, lock acquisition, and foreign calls. A claim about failure preservation must survive the relevant interruptions. It need not survive conditions outside the stated model, such as process termination, unless durability is part of the contract.
Review One Mutation at a Time

Consider transferring an amount between balances. A tempting implementation subtracts from the source and then checks whether the destination can accept the addition. If the second check fails, the source is already changed. Rust prevents many aliasing mistakes here, but it permits this domain error.
The complete implementation below computes every fallible arithmetic result before committing either mutation. Indices are validated before
indexing. Distinctness is explicit. Assignments of the resulting u64 values do not call user code, allocate, or perform arithmetic that could fail.

The mutation appears to occur in two assignments, but no safe observer can read the slice through another live conflicting reference during the exclusive borrow. There is also no callback between the assignments. For
this local in-memory contract, the prepared values are committed without an observable intermediate state through the function's safe interface.

That conclusion would need revision if balances were atomic values observed concurrently, if each assignment wrote a remote database row, or if setting a balance invoked user-defined code. The proof depends on the representation and operations, not merely on the visual proximity of two lines.

The function rejects same-account transfers even for zero amount. That is a policy, and the order of checks makes it take precedence over invalid-index reporting when equal invalid indices are supplied. A reviewer should decide whether that behavior matches the API rather than silently assuming another precedence. Exact error behavior often becomes part of downstream tests.
Use Types to Expose Resource Relationships

Now review a cache. Returning &String from behind a mutex is generally incompatible with releasing the guard: later mutation could remove or replace the entry while the reference remains in use. Returning a guard would preserve access but hold the lock for the caller's entire use. Returning an owned Arc<String> gives the caller an independent ownership share while allowing the map lock to be released.

The next complete program uses this approach. It deliberately permits duplicate loading under contention. That policy avoids holding the lock while executing a potentially slow or reentrant loader. The first installed value wins, and every successful caller receives the stored value.

Reviewing this implementation requires separating three properties. The returned value remains alive because the caller owns an Arc. The map is protected because access occurs while holding the mutex. The loader may execute more than once for one key because it runs outside the lock. None of those properties implies the others.

If duplicate loads have unwanted effects, coordinate one active loader and its waiters per key. Publish failure on panic or abandonment. Releasing the map lock still permits A to wait for B while B waits for A. Give keys a fixed total order and allow each loader to request only higher-ranked keys. Reject other requests before starting or waiting on a load.

The cache is also unbounded. A correct ownership story does not establish an eviction policy. Even with eviction, callers can retain values after the map removes them, so resident-map size and total live payload memory are different metrics. If the application needs a hard memory budget, shared ownership and retained external handles must participate in that budget.

Mutex poisoning is handled here by panicking through unwrap. That is an explicit simplification of the example's recovery contract. A reusable cache should decide whether poisoned state can be inspected and repaired,
discarded, or treated as fatal. Blindly replacing every unwrap with recovery can be as incorrect as blindly adding them, because recovery requires understanding the protected invariant.
Treat Unsafe Boundaries as Proof Boundaries

When unsafe code appears, ask why safe operations cannot express the required implementation and which extra claim the caller or abstraction makes. A raw pointer does not record allocation lifetime, initialized extent, or permitted aliasing. Those facts must come from somewhere: a constructor, a borrow, a foreign contract, or an invariant maintained by earlier operations.

The review should follow pointer creation, transformation, use, and destruction. An index bounds check proves only part of a dereference obligation. The pointer must also have appropriate provenance, alignment, initialization, validity for the accessed type, and compatible aliasing. Creating a reference may impose stronger requirements than merely manipulating a raw pointer. A safety comment should connect the operation to these concrete facts.

Do not assume a private unsafe block is safe because all public methods are safe. A safe abstraction must preserve its invariants for every safe caller, including callers that provide unusual trait implementations, panic in callbacks, forget guards, or pass zero-sized types. If correctness requires a trait implementation to uphold memory safety, an ordinary safe trait bound may be insufficient; the contract needs an appropriate unsafe boundary or additional defensive checks.

Conversely, do not add unsafe code merely to make the borrow checker accept an implementation that can be redesigned safely. A helper using split_at_mut, a separate owner and view, a stable handle, or a staged mutation can often make the proof visible in the types. The best reason to use unsafe is a requirement that has been identified and justified, such as an implementation primitive or measured performance need that safe alternatives cannot meet acceptably.

Compilation checks type relationships, trait obligations, and many ownership constraints. Unit tests check selected outcomes. Property tests explore invariants across generated inputs. Concurrency model checking explores schedules under a modeled set of primitives. Miri can detect certain undefined behaviors in executed paths. Profiling and benchmarks measure particular workloads. Each tool contributes evidence for a different claim.

For the transfer function, useful tests include insufficient funds, destination overflow, invalid indices, same-account policy, and preservation on error. A property can compare the total before and after a successful transfer using a wider integer type. For the cache, use synchronization to arrange two concurrent misses and test the documented winner policy. Counting only successful lookups would miss duplicate loader execution.

For unsafe code, passing tests is not a replacement for the invariant argument. Tests rarely cover every aliasing history, layout, panic point, or target. A successful Miri run means the executed paths passed that tool's checks under its current model; it is not a language-level proof of soundness. The unsettled details of Rust's memory model make precise source references and conservative implementation choices especially important.

Performance claims require their own evidence. A generic iterator chain may optimize well, but that does not establish the application's latency distribution. An allocation-free parser may retain a huge source buffer. A lock-free structure may spend significant time on retries and reclamation. Review the actual workload and the cost that matters to the caller.
Read Compiler Diagnostics as Missing Relationships

An ownership error often says that the program has not expressed a relationship clearly enough. A method borrowing all of self may hide field disjointness. A returned reference may depend on a temporary guard. A spawned task may retain a borrow of a stack frame that can end first. A generic trait object may lack a lifetime or auto-trait bound needed by its consumer.

Before adding a clone, mutex, box, or 'static bound, explain what relationship is missing. Sometimes cloning is exactly right because the consumer needs independent ownership. Sometimes a mutex is right because shared mutation is the requirement. Sometimes a narrower borrow or a handle-based representation is more accurate. The error message is a starting point for that analysis, not a request for one universal repair.

The same discipline applies when code compiles unexpectedly. Nonlexical lifetimes may end a borrow before the end of a block. Reborrowing may temporarily restrict an existing mutable reference without consuming its underlying capability forever. A bound may be satisfied through a blanket implementation. Explain the accepted program in terms of these relationships rather than assuming the compiler overlooked a rule.

First identify the owned resources and the exact points where responsibility transfers. Then identify borrowed views and which mutation or destruction would invalidate them. Next examine state transitions and failures, including cancellation and callbacks. After that inspect concurrency progress and memory bounds. Finally examine public compatibility promises and the evidence supplied by tests and measurements.

This sequence is useful because later questions depend on earlier ones. You cannot assess cancellation correctly without knowing which object owns partial progress. You cannot bound memory without knowing which shared handles retain allocations. You cannot audit a raw pointer without knowing which allocation and lifetime it comes from. Technical vocabulary helps only when it connects these facts.

Rust's concepts become most powerful when used together. Ownership defines responsibility. Borrowing grants temporary access. Traits express obligations and relationships. Enums represent alternatives. Async exposes suspended computations. Pinning constrains movement for address-sensitive values. Unsafe code permits operations whose proof lies outside ordinary checks. A strong design uses each mechanism to express one part of a coherent argument.

1. Generalize transfer to a balance type whose arithmetic can return errors and whose assignment may run a destructor. Identify which parts of the original failure argument no longer follow automatically.
2. Change the cache to return errors and allow one active loader per key. Model loading, ready, and failed. Explain panic cleanup and what happens when two active loaders request each other's keys.

3. Choose a function from your own codebase and write three claims: one enforced by types, one requiring runtime validation, and one requiring a protocol with another component. Name a verification method for each.

1. Fallible arithmetic can still be staged, but replacing old values may invoke destructors that panic or affect external state. A generic rollback promise needs stronger assumptions or a representation that commits by swapping a prepared aggregate with carefully defined destruction behavior. The simple u64 proof cannot be transferred merely by replacing the type parameter.

2. Give each load a shared entry and publish ready or failed once, including when a panic guard cleans up. Wake waiters. Apply the same strict key order to starting nested loads and waiting for existing ones. Every dependency increases in rank, so a cycle would have to increase and return to its starting rank. Test A and B loading together and reject the backwards request before it can block.

3. An example type claim is that a returned view cannot outlive its source, checked through compilation. A runtime claim is that an index is within the initialized prefix, checked through validation and boundary tests. A protocol claim is that retries do not duplicate a remote effect, checked through operation identifiers, peer behavior, and fault-injection tests. No single tool establishes all three.

A Mutable Borrow Appears to Last Too Long

Find the last use of the value derived from the borrow. A returned reference, iterator, guard, or closure can retain access after the method returns. If later code needs that value, ending its borrow earlier would invalidate the use. Otherwise, a smaller scope or explicit drop can clarify the boundary. Nonlexical lifetime analysis follows uses and constraints, not simply the enclosing block.

A second possibility is an overly broad method signature. A helper taking &mut self claims access to the whole object even if its implementation touches one field. Borrowing disjoint fields directly or passing a narrower field reference can expose the independence the caller needs. The helper's body is not normally substituted into every call site for borrow checking.
A Reference Cannot Be Returned From Behind a Guard

Ask who prevents mutation or destruction after the guard is released. Returning the guard preserves synchronization for the caller's use. Returning a copied value or an Arc transfers independent ownership. Running a callback while the guard is held offers temporary access but introduces lock-duration and reentrancy concerns. Returning a bare reference after releasing the only protection generally loses the relationship that made access valid.

The same pattern appears with RefCell guards, mapped file views, transaction snapshots, and temporary owners. Identify the owner or capability that must travel with the view. If no practical return type can carry it, redesign the API around an owned result or scoped operation.
A Spawned Task Requires Static Data

An unscoped task can outlive the stack frame that creates it. A borrow of a local variable cannot support that possibility. Move owned data into the task, share ownership with an appropriate Arc, or use a scoped concurrency mechanism whose lifetime boundary is enforced. A 'static bound on a type means it contains no borrowed data that expires sooner; it does not mean its value must remain alive forever.

Adding move changes how a closure or async block captures its environment. It does not turn a borrowed reference into owned backing storage. A moved &str can still point into a local string. Follow the capture one level deeper and name the actual owner of the bytes.

Inspect the state retained across suspension points. A value that is used and dropped before an await may not enter the suspended state; a value kept across the await does. Common causes include Rc, non-Send guards, trait objects without required auto-trait bounds, and borrowed data whose referent does not satisfy the necessary relationship.

Decide whether thread migration is actually required. A local executor may accept a non-Send future. If migration is required, shorten the lifetime of the offending value, change ownership or synchronization representation, or adjust the trait contract that produces the future. Do not replace every local type with a synchronized equivalent unless shared access is part of the requirement.
A Trait Cannot Be Used as a Dyn Type

Inspect which operations require information unavailable through an erased receiver. Generic methods, unconstrained uses of Self, and associated items can prevent the desired dynamic interface. Sometimes a method can be excluded from dynamic dispatch with an appropriate Self: Sized condition. Sometimes the public trait should be split into a small erased core and a generic extension.
Associated types may need explicit choices in the trait object. Erasure removes the concrete implementing type; it does not remove every
relationship the interface needs. An adapter can package a generic implementation behind a simpler object-safe operation when dynamic composition is a real requirement.

Rust must select a coherent implementation under its overlap rules, including implementations that a blanket rule covers. Adding a more specific implementation does not generally specialize a stable blanket implementation. A newtype creates a distinct type on which a different implementation may be legal. A policy parameter or explicitly named adapter can make the choice visible rather than relying on overlapping inference.

For orphan-rule errors, identify which trait or type is local and how generic parameters appear in the implementation. The rules are more precise than saying that one mentioned type is local. When designing a library, remember that a broad blanket implementation can reserve implementation space that downstream users might otherwise need.
A Lifetime Annotation Does Not Fix a Returned Temporary

An annotation describes a relationship among valid references. It does not extend the storage duration of a local allocation or temporary owner. If a function creates a string and wants to return its contents, return the owned string, place the storage in a caller-provided owner, or use another representation whose owner survives.

When the return value genuinely borrows from an input, make that relationship explicit enough for the compiler and caller. Avoid assigning one lifetime to every parameter merely to make the signature shorter. Unrelated inputs can then become unnecessarily coupled, restricting calls that should be valid.
An Iterator Cannot Yield the Borrow You Expected

Determine whether each item borrows from the iterator's original backing data or from the current mutable borrow of the iterator itself. Ordinary Iterator has one associated Item type for the implementation. A lending interface can use a generic associated type tied to each call, which prevents retaining one item while requesting another when the buffer is reused.

Changing to owned items is sometimes the right API, especially when consumers need to retain them. Collecting borrowed items from a reused buffer is not fixed by annotation because it conflicts with the storage policy. Decide whether the producer or consumer should own the retained bytes.
Pin Does Not Permit a Field Operation

Ask whether the field is structurally pinned and whether exposing a pinned projection is part of the type's contract. A pinned outer value does not automatically authorize arbitrary projection, replacement, or movement of its fields. Unpin changes which restrictions matter, and a pointer wrapper's movability is different from moving its pointee.

Use a documented safe projection facility where appropriate. If implementing projection with unsafe code, explain why the projected value remains pinned until its required destruction and why no other safe operation can move it. Address stability is a whole-abstraction promise, not a one-line cast property.

Separate the syntax of a const context from the operations permitted during compile-time evaluation. A function callable at runtime is not necessarily callable in const evaluation. A const generic parameter does not make every arithmetic expression over that parameter legal in every type position on stable Rust.

Consider whether the computation truly belongs in the type system. A constructor that validates a runtime value may offer a simpler contract. If compile-time evaluation is required, use supported const operations and
represent constraints within the stable feature set rather than silently requiring nightly behavior.
A Safe Wrapper Still Needs an Unsafe Trait

If an implementation may cause memory unsafety when a caller supplies a trait implementation that violates a semantic rule, ordinary safe implementors cannot be trusted to uphold that rule for safety. Either validate defensively, avoid depending on that semantic property for memory safety, or place the obligation behind an appropriately documented unsafe trait boundary.

An ordinary trait may still specify semantic laws such as ordering consistency, and violating them may produce logic errors. The critical distinction is whether violating the law can make safe caller code trigger undefined behavior. Review every place the implementation converts semantic expectations into unchecked memory operations.
A Program Compiles but Hangs During Shutdown

Inventory every owner that can keep a resource live. A forgotten channel sender prevents a receiver from observing disconnection. A guard held while joining a thread may prevent that thread from acquiring its lock. A result queue that is no longer drained can keep workers blocked while the coordinator waits for them to exit.

Draw the wait graph and the ownership graph separately. Memory safety can hold while the wait graph contains a cycle. Define which component closes admission, which drains accepted work, which drops the final sender, and which observes completion. Test shutdown as a protocol rather than as incidental cleanup.
A Clone Fixes Compilation but Memory Grows

Inspect what was cloned. Cloning a String duplicates bytes. Cloning an Arc duplicates a handle and retains the underlying allocation. Cloning a snapshot can preserve an entire historical structure. A cheap clone may therefore be expensive in lifetime and peak memory even when its immediate CPU cost is small.

Measure live retained data under the actual workload. A small selective copy can release a much larger shared source. A bounded queue containing shared handles can still retain large allocations. Decide whether independent ownership, shared retention, or a narrower borrowed scope matches the consumer's requirement.
