Appendix B A Glossary of Relationships
Each entry names the relationship behind a term. Use the topic index for the chapter that develops its rules, examples, and limits.

A state whose correctness depends on a value remaining at a particular memory location. Self references and intrusive links are examples. Pinning can support an address-stability contract, but the implementation must still establish and preserve the relevant invariant.

Ownership described as at-most-once consumption of a value through a particular noncopyable binding, with discarding also permitted. Rust does not generally require each value to be used exactly once or guarantee that every destructor executes.

Multiple access paths that can reach overlapping storage. Whether particular accesses are permitted depends on reference and pointer rules, interior mutability, liveness, and the operations performed. The mere existence of two addresses is not a complete aliasing analysis.

A type selected by an implementation of a trait for a particular implementation relationship. It lets an interface describe connected types, such as an iterator and its item, without making every use choose an independent type parameter.

A trait whose implementation is often derived structurally from a type's components, subject to the trait's rules and explicit implementations. Send, Sync, and Unpin are central examples. Auto-trait behavior can become part of a public type's compatibility surface.

Temporary access to a value under constraints that preserve valid use. A borrow relates the access to an owner and to potentially conflicting operations. It does not transfer the owner's ordinary responsibility for the borrowed resource.

A value or access relationship that grants a particular operation. An exclusive reference grants access under exclusivity constraints; a typestate value may grant permission to send protocol data. The interpretation is useful only when construction and duplication preserve the intended authority.

The set of rules that allows trait implementation selection to remain unambiguous across crates. Overlap checks and orphan rules shape which implementations may exist. A broad implementation can restrict future implementation choices even when its current body is small.

A relationship in which substituting a subtype reverses direction through a type constructor. Function argument positions provide an important example. Variance describes permitted substitutions; it does not mean the compiler can arbitrarily lengthen the lifetime of actual storage.

A relationship in which subtype substitution is preserved through a type constructor. Shared references are covariant over relevant parameters. This supports shortening a usable lifetime when appropriate, while preserving the requirement that the underlying value remains valid.

Compiler analysis that considers whether borrowed data may still be accessed when an owning value's destructor runs. The fact that ordinary methods no longer use a reference does not always end the relationship relevant to destruction.

A conceptual or implementation mechanism for tracking whether a place currently contains an initialized value requiring destruction. Conditional initialization and partial moves require cleanup behavior to depend on which values actually exist at the cleanup point.

The conditions under which a trait can support a trait-object interface. Erased dispatch must have enough information to invoke permitted methods without knowing the concrete implementing type. Some trait operations cannot be represented through that interface.

Hiding a concrete type behind an interface that preserves selected operations and bounds. A trait object erases the implementor while retaining its trait contract, associated choices, lifetime constraints, and requested auto traits. Erasure is a design boundary rather than the absence of types.

Access whose validity depends on restricting conflicting access paths for the relevant duration. &mut T is the principal safe-language expression of this relationship. Exclusivity can matter even when an operation performs no write.

A value representing a computation that can be polled toward completion. It may retain local state and borrows between polls. Creating a future does not generally execute its async body to completion or assign it an operating-system thread.
An associated type that has its own generic parameters. A lending interface can use a lifetime parameter to connect each returned item to the particular borrow of the producer used by that call.

An ordering relationship used to reason about effects across threads, assembled from the relevant sequencing and synchronization rules. Atomicity alone does not establish every required edge. An ordering proof must identify the actual operations that publish and observe state.

A bound quantified over a family of lifetimes, commonly written with for<'a>. It can require a callback or trait relationship to work for every lifetime selected under that quantification rather than one lifetime chosen by the caller.

Mutation made available through shared access under an abstraction's rules. UnsafeCell supports the core language exception, while types such as Cell, RefCell, and synchronization primitives impose different safe access protocols. Shared access does not thereby authorize arbitrary unsynchronized mutation.

A relationship that does not permit subtype substitution through the relevant parameter. Mutable access and interior-mutability representations often require invariance over stored types so one lifetime or type choice cannot be replaced by an incompatible one.

An interface pattern in which an output borrows from the producer's current access, often preventing another operation while that output remains in use. It supports reusable internal storage whose contents cannot safely back several simultaneously retained items.

A constraint on which borrowed data a type or reference may contain and how long it may be used. A lifetime annotation expresses a relationship; it does not allocate storage, extend a local variable's existence, or run a destructor.

Generating specialized code for concrete generic instantiations. It can expose optimization opportunities and increase code size or compilation work. The resulting machine-code cost depends on optimization and usage rather than on generic syntax alone.

A borrow-analysis behavior in which relevant uses and control-flow constraints can determine the borrow's duration more precisely than the enclosing lexical block. It explains why an owner can sometimes be mutated after a reference's last use within the same block.

A contract that constrains movement of a pointee once the relevant promise is established, including obligations around destruction. Moving a pinned pointer handle is different from moving its pointee. Projection determines which fields participate in structural pinning.

An expression category describing a storage location, such as a local variable, field, or indexed element. Moves, borrows, assignments, and partial initialization operate on places. Distinguishing a place from a produced value clarifies many ownership rules.

A synchronization mechanism that records a possible invariant interruption after a panic while protected state is accessed. It is advisory evidence for a recovery decision. Clearing or ignoring poison does not itself repair the application's invariant.

Information associated with pointers that concerns their origin and permitted relationship to allocations and accesses. An address alone is not a complete description of permission to dereference. Exact pointer operations must follow their documented contracts and Rust's evolving memory-model requirements.

A borrow created through an existing reference, often with a shorter usable duration. It can temporarily grant access while restricting use of the original reference. This allows mutable references to participate in repeated calls without being permanently consumed each time.

The layout and ABI-related choices for values, including size, alignment, field placement, and discriminants where specified. A representation attribute provides particular guarantees; it does not automatically validate bytes or make an arbitrary Rust type safe for every foreign interface.

An abstraction whose safe use cannot cause undefined behavior when its unsafe implementation's obligations and documented unsafe caller contracts are respected. Soundness is stronger than passing tests and different from being free of ordinary logic errors.

A choice that a field participates in its enclosing type's pinning guarantee. Exposing a pinned projection commits the implementation to preserving that relationship across mutation, destruction, and Unpin behavior. It is not an automatic property of every field.

A relationship permitting one type to be used where another is required under language rules. Lifetime subtyping and variance are important in Rust. Subtyping should not be confused with inheritance of data fields or arbitrary implicit conversion.

Representing a resource's protocol phase through types so different operations are available in different phases. Consuming transitions can prevent reuse of an old capability. Runtime state machines remain useful when states must be stored or selected dynamically.

Behavior outside the program's permitted language and library contracts, invalidating ordinary reasoning about the resulting execution. Unsafe blocks do not make undefined behavior acceptable. Preventing it requires satisfying all relevant validity, access, lifetime, concurrency, and boundary obligations.

An auto trait indicating that a type does not need the pinning restriction for soundness. It allows safe pinned access to recover ordinary mutable access in applicable APIs. It concerns the pointee's requirements rather than whether a pointer handle itself can move.

The requirements for bytes and metadata to constitute an allowed value of a type. A valid allocation and sufficient size do not imply a valid bool, reference, enum, or string. Creating a typed value may impose obligations before any later semantic use.

A handle through which a task can be scheduled for another poll after relevant progress becomes possible. A wake is a notification, not the result itself and not necessarily a one-to-one request for an immediate poll. Correct registration must avoid lost notifications.

A type whose values require zero bytes of storage, though the type still has alignment and semantic behavior. Such values can participate in ownership, destruction, and generic algorithms. Zero size does not justify ignoring the contracts of references, pointers, or allocators.
Page numbers identify field manual openings. Each entry links to the relevant field manual.

Async Service Lab From Pending to

The wakeup and service chapters study one obligation at a time. This lab joins them in one complete program: a caller submits owned work, polls a reply, cancels or expires work at a checkpoint, closes admission, and observes the worker's termination. It uses only the standard library and runs offline.

This is a controlled service model, not a network runtime. One worker owns execution, one permit bounds unfinished accepted work, and a future represents the caller's reply. A test controller pauses the worker at a checkpoint so every run can exercise a real Pending-to-Ready transition without sleeps. Its integer clock advances only when the controller changes it. A production service would use its runtime's monotonic clock, timer and cancellation facilities.

The service owns its worker handle and request sender. A Job owns the admission permit until the worker records an outcome. The worker and Operation share reply state; that state stores either a result or the current waker. Control belongs to the test driver. Its release message lets the worker cross the checkpoint, and its acknowledgement lets the driver check a known schedule.

caller -> admission -> Job owns permit -> worker checkpoint
caller polls Operation -> registers waker -> Pending
test chooses clock/cancel -> releases worker
worker records outcome -> drops permit -> wakes -> acknowledges
caller polls -> Ready; owner closes input and joins worker

The reply lock makes readiness and registration one decision. The executor's separate predicate preserves a wake delivered before it waits. Neither mutex is held while invoking a waker. Cancellation takes priority over deadline expiry in this lab; both are checked before the arithmetic operation.

Save this listing as async_service_lab.rs. Compile with rustc --edition=2024 async_service_lab.rs -o async_service_lab.exe, then run the executable. On a non-Windows host, choose an output name without the .exe suffix. Every assertion describes part of the contract.

The worker cannot pass its checkpoint before Control releases or disconnects it. The first poll therefore registers a waker and returns Pending. The driver's hook changes policy inputs, releases the worker, and waits for its acknowledgement. The worker records the result, releases the permit, and wakes before sending that acknowledgement. The next poll is Ready. The assertion of exactly two polls checks this controlled schedule, not a general promise that every future needs two polls.

The readiness predicate survives the driver's wait. Replacing it with an assumption that a notification will occur after waiting begins would lose this wake-before-wait case. The cancellation and clock atomics are independent policy values; they do not publish a separate data structure. The release channel also orders the controller's preceding actions before the worker crosses the checkpoint.

Closing admission and joining have different jobs. Closure rejects new requests; joining observes the worker finish. A caller can drop Operation while the job continues under the service's ownership. Dropping Control instead disconnects the checkpoint and produces a cancellation result. Every demonstrated path releases its permit, including checked-arithmetic failure.
State the Limits Before Extending It

This lab bounds unfinished accepted work, not the number of completed replies a caller may retain. It has one worker, no external effects and no process-crash recovery. Its checkpoint is test machinery, not an I/O interface. A logical deadline chooses an outcome at that checkpoint; it does not preempt a blocking call or impose a wall-clock bound on shutdown. Progress still assumes the worker is scheduled and the controller releases or drops its checkpoint capability.

Call shutdown to observe termination. Merely dropping a JoinHandle detaches its thread; Rust does not force the owner to call this method. Lock poisoning and worker panic use fail-fast unwrap calls here. A reusable service must classify those failures, define abandoned reply cleanup, and decide how to handle uncertain external effects. The small executor is unsuitable for futures that require another runtime's reactor.

First remove the shared readiness predicate from the executor. Explain the schedule above in which a wake occurs before the wait, and why a transient notification alone cannot carry that fact. Restore the predicate before continuing.

Next move permit release to the caller's Operation destructor. Use the abandoned-caller case to explain how that would free capacity while work still exists. Keep accounting with the worker instead. Finally add a second bounded processing phase and carry the same absolute logical deadline into it; do not grant a fresh budget merely because the job crossed a function boundary.
Lab D One Request Across the Dispatch

The final campaign asks you to combine the parser, store, worker pipeline, and protocol chapters. This worked bridge follows one request through those boundaries before you build your own variation. The service accepts a small command such as K7=12: perform twelve units of work under operation identifier K7.

The program is a finite, process-local simulator. The peer is a separate object so its state can change even when the caller loses the acknowledgment. It is not a network server, database, or durable queue. Its serial coordinator makes each state transition inspectable. The async service lab supplies the complementary executable ownership and shutdown example.

input String
  | parse: borrow id, validate units
  v
Request<'_> -- into_job --> owned Job
                              |
                   revision + admission check
                              v
                    pending ledger + queue
                              |
                   peer applies stable id
                         /           \
                      reply         reply lost
                        |               |
                       Done          Unknown
                                        |
                          same-id status lookup
                                        v
                              Done or still Unknown
Parsing borrows the identifier, so it adds no owned string. Converting to Job copies only that identifier; the request buffer can then be released. The
numeric payload is canonical: K7=012 and K7=12 mean the same request. A repeated identifier with a different numeric payload is a conflict.

Admission is the point at which the coordinator records responsibility. At each public method boundary, every accepted request has exactly one ledger entry. Each unfinished entry also has exactly one queued owner. Capacity counts unfinished work, including uncertain outcomes, rather than only the jobs that have not yet been sent. Completed receipts remain in a separately bounded ledger.

This program uses only the standard library. Run the supplied source with edition 2024. Its assertions cover stale proposals, full admission, changed payloads, lost acknowledgment, replay, shutdown, and unresolved work.

K7 is borrowed from the input, converted to an owned Job, and admitted under revision zero. A stale proposal for K8 is rejected with the original Job. Retrying that local proposal against the new revision succeeds because it has not caused an external effect. This is different from retrying K7 after losing the peer's reply.

The first step applies K7 at the peer and records Unknown locally. Another K7 submission returns Busy with the caller's Job; it does not send again. K7 with a changed payload is rejected. Closing admission then sends K8 and queries the existing K7 identity. The peer's receipt resolves K7 without producing another effect. The final report accounts for both accepted requests.

The second service cannot obtain status. Its bounded drain returns with one Unknown and does not claim to have stopped. A real shutdown deadline needs a policy for persisting, handing off, or escalating that responsibility. Dropping this simulator would lose its local records; no destructor can make them durable.

The last assertion sequence is the broken policy: after a lost reply, create a new key. The peer sees two independent operations and records two effects. This is a semantic counterexample, executed safely; it does not rely on a race or on undefined behavior.

The coordinator serializes proposals and revisions through &mut self. The revision covers the local ledger and admission decision, not the independent peer. Each record changes at most three times, and only four records can be admitted, so the revision cannot overflow in this finite model. New queue insertions stay within its preallocated capacity. The example assumes standard allocations succeed and contains no user callbacks during local publication; it does not promise recovery from allocator abort or arbitrary injected panics.

There is no operating-system thread or hidden scheduler in this model. No public call can observe the short interval in which step holds the popped Job. A concurrent implementation must put its shared admission state
under an appropriate synchronization protocol and keep ownership with the actual worker until its terminal disposition is recorded. Lab S explores that admission/shutdown boundary.

The peer contract is also explicit: it retains each identifier, binds it to the numeric payload, and makes status available when configured to do so. A real peer may have finite retention, unavailable status, permanent rejection, or different tenant scopes. Those conditions need additional states and a documented reconciliation policy. This model establishes neither cross-process durability nor exactly-once execution in an arbitrary distributed system.

Keep the same boundaries and change one requirement: let the peer's status remain unavailable while new input continues arriving. Decide how much uncertain work you will retain, when admission must close, and which component owns escalation. Write the accepted-work accounting equation before extending the code. Preserve the original assertions and add a case that would fail if an Unknown were silently counted as Done.

Stress tests can miss a bad schedule even when every operation is memory safe. This lab makes the scheduling choices explicit. An admission participant checks whether a service is open and then registers one active request. A shutdown participant closes admission and decides whether zero active requests means it can report Stopped.

The broken implementation separates the check from registration. Its report can be correct at the instant of observation and become false when a request registers afterward. The invariant we want is: once Stopped is reported, no request can become active.

Each participant preserves its own operation order. Interleaving two admission steps with two shutdown steps gives six histories. The complete program enumerates all six and finds one that violates the invariant. The repair groups the open check and registration into one admission transition. Interleaving that transition with the two shutdown steps gives three histories; all preserve the modeled invariant.

step   participant   observation or change
1      admission     remembers open = true
2      shutdown      open becomes false
3      shutdown      sees active = 0, reports Stopped
4      admission     uses old check, active becomes 1

No individual read has to be a data race for this protocol to fail. Putting separate reads and writes behind separate lock acquisitions can still permit this history. The repair must protect the relationship between checking open and increasing the active count. In a mutex design, both happen while holding the same guard; shutdown uses that mutex when it closes intake and observes the count.

The three repaired histories have straightforward meanings. If Admit runs first, the count is one and shutdown must wait. If Close runs first, Admit rejects the request. Moving Observe before or after that rejected Admit cannot create active work after Stopped. The model does not assert that shutdown finishes while accepted work remains.
Keep the Conclusion Inside the Model

This is a hand-written sequential state explorer, not Loom and not an implementation of Rust's memory model. It exhausts only the listed atomic transitions for one request and one shutdown. The grouping of Admit is an assumption that the implementation must justify with synchronization. Merely naming a function Admit would not make its body atomic.

The model has no completion, cancellation, capacity, panic, or notification transitions. It proves no fairness or liveness result and tests no weak-memory behavior. Extend the model when one of those facts participates in the real invariant. A completed task also needs a correct decrement and a notification protocol that cannot lose a wakeup; that is separate evidence from rejecting late admission.

For a larger implementation, a tool such as Loom can explore interleavings using its modeled synchronization primitives. Follow the tool's requirements and limitations, including its relaxed-memory caveats and
state-space bounds. A passing bounded model supports its modeled claim; it does not certify every safe caller or every deployment.

Add a completion event and allow shutdown to observe the count both before and after completion. Define which transition can publish Stopped, and assert that no accepted request is lost. Then add a waiter-registration step and look for a lost wakeup. Do not use a sleep as a substitute for either transition: the useful output is a reproducible history and an invariant that explains the repair.
